subject: Immunology
vignette: A 44-year-old woman presents with 6 months of symmetric stiffness and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, along with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour. She also has fatigue. Examination shows soft, boggy swelling of the MCP and PIP joints, sparing the distal interphalangeal joints, and ulnar deviation of the fingers. Labs: elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, positive rheumatoid factor, and positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Radiographs show periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions.
question: Which of the following is the most characteristic structural feature of the pathogenic lesion in this disease?

options.text: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells in the synovium
Microcrystalline deposits in the joint space with chondrocalcinosis
Villous hypertrophy of the synovium with formation of a pannus that erodes cartilage and bone
Cholesterol crystals in the synovial fluid

explanation_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic immune-mediated synovitis driven by CD4+ T cell activation, cytokine production (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6), and B cell autoantibody production. The inflamed synovium becomes hypertrophic and forms a pannus, an invasive granulation tissue that erodes cartilage and subchondral bone, producing the marginal erosions seen on radiographs. Symmetric involvement of small joints with sparing of the DIP joints and prolonged morning stiffness are hallmarks of the disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Granulomatous synovitis with giant cells is not the primary lesion of RA; rheumatoid nodules are necrotizing granulomas occurring subcutaneously or in organs.
explanation_incorrect.B: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition causes pseudogout with chondrocalcinosis, typically affecting the knee and wrist with acute attacks.
explanation_incorrect.D: Monosodium urate tophi are features of gout, producing episodic monoarthritis, often of the first MTP joint.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholesterol crystals are found in chronic effusions and some bursitis but are not the characteristic lesion of rheumatoid arthritis.

educationalObjective: Rheumatoid arthritis produces a proliferative synovial pannus that erodes cartilage and bone at joint margins.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 38-year-old woman with seropositive, anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis has had persistent synovitis despite methotrexate and low-dose prednisone for 6 months. Her joint count remains high and CRP is elevated. She is otherwise well, with no evidence of infection or malignancy, and has no prior history of tuberculosis or hepatitis.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Begin a course of high-dose cyclophosphamide
Add colchicine to reduce inflammatory flares
Switch to allopurinol for long-term disease control
Add a monoclonal antibody against CD20 on plasma cells
Add a TNF-alpha inhibitor such as etanercept after screening for latent tuberculosis

explanation_correct: In patients with inadequate response to conventional synthetic disease-modifying therapy such as methotrexate, adding a biologic DMARD is indicated. TNF-alpha inhibitors (etanercept is a soluble TNF receptor fusion protein, while infliximab and adalimumab are anti-TNF antibodies) are first-line biologics because TNF drives synovial inflammation, matrix metalloproteinase production, and osteoclast activation. Patients must be screened for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before anti-TNF therapy, and methotrexate is typically continued in combination.

explanation_incorrect.A: High-dose cyclophosphamide is used for severe vasculitis or catastrophic autoimmune disease and carries risks that are not justified in RA.
explanation_incorrect.B: Colchicine is used for gout and pericarditis and does not alter the immune disease course of rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Allopurinol lowers uric acid and treats gout; it has no role in the management of rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells, not plasma cells (which are CD20 negative), and is reserved for patients who fail TNF inhibitors.

educationalObjective: After inadequate response to methotrexate, TNF-alpha inhibitors are the preferred next-line biologic DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 56-year-old man with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, poorly controlled for 15 years, presents with 6 months of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough. He has never smoked and has no occupational exposures. Examination reveals bibasilar fine crackles and mild clubbing. Chest CT shows basilar-predominant reticular opacities and honeycombing. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity.
question: Which of the following best explains this pulmonary complication?

options.text: Necrotizing granulomas with cavitation in the upper lobes
Antibody deposition along the alveolar basement membrane causing pulmonary hemorrhage
Chronic immune-mediated fibrosing interstitial lung disease associated with severe, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
Mediastinal lymphadenopathy with bilateral hilar enlargement

explanation_correct: Interstitial lung disease is a serious extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, presenting as usual interstitial pneumonia with basilar reticulation, honeycombing, and a restrictive ventilatory defect. Risk is higher in men, smokers, and those with high-titer anti-CCP or rheumatoid factor and long-standing erosive disease; his anti-CCP positivity and 15-year erosive course place him at high risk even without smoking. Notably, citrullination of proteins is thought to occur in the lung mucosa, making pulmonary disease a manifestation of the same autoimmunity. Rheumatoid nodules and pleural effusion are other thoracic manifestations.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cavitating upper-lobe granulomas are typical of tuberculosis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not the interstitial fibrosis pattern described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Alveolar basement membrane antibody deposition describes Goodpasture disease, which causes hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis, not honeycombing.
explanation_incorrect.C: Eosinophilic infiltration with asthma characterizes eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and would show peripheral eosinophilia and obstructive physiology.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with fever is typical of sarcoidosis and is not the pattern of rheumatoid-associated interstitial lung disease.

educationalObjective: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause fibrosing interstitial lung disease, particularly in male smokers with high-titer anti-CCP and severe erosive disease.
